The preliminary results of a study suggest that the condition of the cell microenvironment of mediastinal lymph nodes can potentially help predict the risk of metastases in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). This approach may be useful as an independent tumor staging factor, although part of the staging process could also be based on features describing the immune cells in the peripheral blood. However, it is essential to note that more research is needed to confirm this finding and its implications for clinical practice.

The study found that patients with lower metastasis rates in their mediastinal lymph nodes had a better prognosis, while those with higher metastasis rates did not show a significant advantage in terms of survival rate. Additionally, the presence of certain immune cells in the peripheral blood may provide valuable information about the likelihood of cancer progression and metastasis.

Overall, this study suggests that monitoring the cell microenvironment of mediastinal lymph nodes could be a useful tool for predicting the risk of metastases in NSCLC patients. Further research is needed to confirm these findings and explore their potential applications in clinical practice.
